explanation: Traffic law obligates every person using the road—drivers, pedestrians, cyclists, and passengers alike—to know and follow the traffic rules, not drivers alone.
A person may only drive a motor vehicle if they hold a valid driver's license issued for that specific vehicle class; the license-class match is the legal precondition for driving.

The owner or person controlling a vehicle has a legal duty to prevent anyone from driving it who lacks a valid license for that type of vehicle, since the owner is responsible for who takes the wheel.

Regulation sets two alternative experience-and-age thresholds for a lawful escort: a same-class license held for at least five years with the escort aged 24 or over, or held for at least three years with the escort aged 30 or over.

A police officer may detain a driver without a warrant specifically when the driver fails to give their name and address or refuses to present their license as legally required, since identification is the officer's basis for proceeding.
A 30-day license revocation applies when a driver's conduct endangers a person on a pedestrian crossing, reflecting the extra legal protection given to pedestrians at crossings.

A 60-day revocation is triggered when a driver involved in an accident is reasonably suspected of causing injury to a person or damage to property, a lower threshold than proof of guilt but enough for immediate precaution.
The most severe 90-day revocation applies when a driver involved in an accident is reasonably suspected of causing a person's death, reflecting the seriousness of a fatal outcome.

Driving while disqualified is treated as a serious offense under traffic law, carrying up to three years imprisonment in addition to other penalties, because it defies a formal order removing driving privileges.
The legal definition of a road is deliberately broad, covering any rail, street, alley, square, passage, or bridge where the public has a right to pass, not only paved city streets.
Lighting up time is legally defined as night hours or any other time when weather or similar conditions reduce visibility enough that vehicle lights are needed, not merely a fixed clock period.
Parking is legally defined as standing a vehicle for an uninterrupted period that is not for the immediate loading or unloading of passengers or goods, which is what separates it from a mere stop.
A utility tractor is defined by specific technical criteria: at least four wheels, an all-up weight capped at 1,500 kg, and steering by a wheel rather than a handlebar.
An ATV is legally defined by having at least four wheels with the rider seated astride the vehicle and steering it using handlebars, distinguishing it from wheel-steered vehicles.
No-stopping sign 433 posted on the right of a two-way road prohibits stopping on the right side of the roadway itself and on the adjoining hard shoulder, since both are part of that side of the road.
A one-way street is legally defined as a roadway in which vehicle traffic is permitted in only one direction, tying the definition specifically to the paved roadway rather than any path.
Night time is legally defined as the period beginning 15 minutes after sunset and ending 15 minutes before sunrise, a fixed buffer rather than the full sunset-to-sunrise span.
By law the pavement is reserved for pedestrian use; vehicles, including bicycles and motorcycles, are not permitted to use it as an alternative to the roadway.
An interchange is defined as a meeting point of roads at different levels connected in a way that allows drivers to pass from one road to the other, unlike a same-level junction.
Permitted load refers strictly to the maximum weight of cargo, measured in kilograms, that a commercial vehicle is licensed to carry, separate from the vehicle's own weight.
The boundary of a junction is fixed by the imaginary line drawn between the pavements or kerbs of the roads that meet there, giving a precise legal edge to where the junction begins.
Traffic law places responsibility on both the driver and the passenger for ensuring a back-seat passenger wears their seatbelt, so failing to buckle up exposes both to liability.
A pedestrian crossing is defined as a part of the road itself, not the pavement, that is designated and marked for pedestrians to cross.
A level crossing is legally defined as a point where a road and a railroad meet or cross at the same grade, distinguishing it from crossings at different levels such as bridges.
All up weight is defined as the vehicle's own weight plus the maximum weight of people and cargo it is licensed to carry, as approved by the Licensing Authority.
Own weight is the vehicle's base weight alone, excluding any cargo and excluding the driver, which is what distinguishes it from all up weight.
Giving right of way means letting other drivers continue their movement without forcing them to change speed or stop, which is the practical test for whether right of way was actually granted.

Overtaking two vehicles in a single maneuver is allowed whenever overtaking is not otherwise prohibited at that location and the maneuver can be completed safely, following the general rules governing all overtaking.
An axle is technically defined as a shaft or system of shafts running the width of the vehicle and attached to the wheels, a structural definition distinct from engine or body parts.
A road user is defined broadly as anyone using the road for driving, traveling, riding, walking, standing, or any other purpose, not only those operating a vehicle.
To dip the lights specifically means switching from high beam down to low beam, the standard action taken to avoid dazzling oncoming or leading drivers.
A junction is defined simply as the meeting point of two or more roads, without requiring a specific surface type or urban setting.

A stop line is defined generally as a line, full or partial width, marking a stopping point for vehicles, which applies wherever a stop is legally required and not only at signal-controlled junctions.
A play street is legally defined as a road designed for children's games as well as pedestrian and vehicle use, identified by the specific play-street sign posted at its entrance.
A rigid vehicle body is one in which the driver's compartment and the cargo trunk form a single continuous unit, distinguishing it from articulated or separated-body vehicles.
A slow-moving vehicle is legally defined by having a maximum permitted speed capped at 40 km/h or less, which is why lower speed limits and overtaking caution apply around such vehicles.

A vehicle only counts legally as an emergency vehicle when it is an authorized type, such as an ambulance, police, IDF, or fire vehicle, and is actively sounding its alarm and operating its flashing emergency lights.

Carrying passengers for hire in a private passenger car is simply not permitted, since fare-paying transport requires a vehicle licensed for public or commercial use, and no private contract can substitute for that license.
For a private passenger car, the law defines an obsolete vehicle as one manufactured more than 19 years ago, a fixed age threshold rather than a condition-based test.
A private passenger car is legally defined as a private motor vehicle designed to carry up to eight passengers besides the driver and registered on its license as a private vehicle.

Once a vehicle is disqualified from use, it is forbidden to be on the road again without authorization from the Licensing Authority, since the disqualification remains in force until officially lifted.
A path is legally distinguished from a road by being a lane or part of a lane that is not itself a road and is designated for specific users, such as pedestrians or cyclists.
The law makes using another person as a guide while reversing a permitted practice rather than an absolute requirement, leaving the decision to the driver based on the situation's difficulty.
Before getting out of a parked car, the driver has a duty of care to verify that opening the door and exiting will not disturb or endanger any other road user.
A built dividing area is defined as a separation area that divides the road lengthwise by means of an elevated physical structure, distinguishing it from a merely painted or marked division.

A safety seat must meet a defined standard, be secured to the vehicle using a seatbelt, and restrain the child with the seat's own independent harness, which is what separates it from a simple booster.
A booster seat is designed to raise a small child so that the vehicle's own seatbelt can properly restrain them, rather than providing its own separate harness.
A motor vehicle is legally defined broadly as any vehicle propelled by any power or mechanical means, not limited to a particular fuel or engine type.
The law requires a driver to carry a valid driving license, the vehicle's registration, a compulsory insurance certificate, and any other document lawfully required to be held while driving.
Photocopies of vehicle documents may substitute for originals only when the vehicle belongs to a corporation and the copies bear the authorizing signature and stamp of the safety officer.
A driver must produce the vehicle's original documents to a policeman at whatever time and place the officer determines, since a photocopy alone does not satisfy this legal duty.
The points system exists to record demerit points against drivers convicted of traffic-regulation offenses, allowing repeat offenders to be identified and addressed.
The law requires that the driver's and the vehicle's documents always be kept inside the car, clean and readable, so they can be produced properly whenever needed.
The new-driver sign must be placed on the bottom edge of the vehicle's rear window so it is clearly visible to traffic driving behind the vehicle.
A new driver must display the sign for two years, or for as long as new-driver status applies, whichever period is relevant to that individual driver.
Only the Licensing Authority is legally empowered to make changes to the details recorded in a vehicle's or driver's official documents; no self-made alterations are permitted.

A driver must report specific health changes to the Licensing Authority, including detection of heart disease or limitations affecting the nervous system, bones, eyesight, or hearing, since these directly affect fitness to drive.
Traffic signs bind every road user, not only vehicle drivers, since signs regulate the conduct of all people using the road, including pedestrians.
Traffic light signals take priority over right-of-way giving signs, with the single exception of a flashing yellow light, in which case the applicable priority sign governs instead.
The directions and signals of a uniformed policeman must always be obeyed, though drivers should exercise extra caution when following them.
Once a policeman has properly identified themselves, their directions must be obeyed even when they contradict a posted road sign, since a live traffic direction overrides the static sign.
A uniformed municipal inspector's directions are binding specifically when those directions relate to traffic control, giving inspectors limited but real authority over road users.
A uniformed Public Works Department employee's directions must be obeyed wherever road pavement or maintenance works are being conducted, since they are managing safety around the worksite.
A uniformed military policeman's directions and signals carry the same binding legal force as those of a civilian police officer.
A policeman's directions must be obeyed even when they oppose a posted traffic sign, though drivers should proceed with full caution given the potential conflict.
The same rule extends to a military policeman: their directions must be obeyed with full caution even when they contradict the traffic signs in place.
An authorized municipal inspector's directions must likewise be obeyed with full caution even when they conflict with the posted traffic signs.
A temporary sign posted under a police officer's direction is legally regarded as a legitimate traffic sign, carrying the same binding force as a permanent one.
When both traffic signs and traffic lights are present at an intersection, the traffic light's signals take priority over a right-of-way giving sign, except during a flashing yellow phase.
Holding a valid license for a vehicle group permits driving vehicles in that group only when the driver can actually operate and use that particular vehicle proficiently.
It is forbidden to drive whenever a person's physical or mental state might endanger other road users, regardless of whether their license itself remains valid.
Driving is simply not permitted immediately after taking medication that affects a person's fitness to drive, without any exception based on the medication's type.
It is forbidden to drive an un-roadworthy vehicle when its condition means the driver cannot maintain full control over it, since control of the vehicle is the underlying safety concern.
Driving with a restricted front field of vision is prohibited unless the restriction is only negligible, since clear forward visibility is essential to safe control of the vehicle.

A driver may take one hand off the wheel only briefly for necessary actions like changing gears or operating the direction indicator, or to ensure the vehicle's proper function, not for other purposes.
A cellular phone may only be operated while driving through a hands-free device installed in the vehicle that can be used without being held in the hand.
A driver is obliged to wear eyeglasses or contact lenses whenever their driver's license carries that condition, regardless of the time of day or lighting.
Driving through a play street requires allowing pedestrians and children to continue their activities without endangering them, since the street is specifically designated for their use.
A private passenger car is restricted to using the roadway section of the street wherever a roadway exists, and may not use the pavement or separation area even in heavy traffic.
A cyclist is permitted to use a public transportation lane specifically when that lane runs along the right side of the roadway.
The requirement to drive along the road's farthest right side applies universally, across every type of road, not merely on one-way or two-way roads specifically.

The label 3 in the illustration marks the roadway, the paved section of the wide road built and marked for vehicle traffic, as distinct from the pavement, hard shoulder, or dividing area shown alongside it.
A central divider is by default an area where parking is prohibited, unless a specific traffic sign expressly permits otherwise.
On a road split by a central divider, vehicles must keep to the right of the divider by default, unless signage specifically directs otherwise.
A continuous white dividing line requires vehicles to stay strictly on their own right side of the line at all times, since a solid line prohibits crossing even to overtake.
Driving against traffic on a one-way street is prohibited, except for a security vehicle actively on duty or when a policeman directs otherwise.
Driving on the pavement is permitted only for the specific purpose of crossing it in order to enter or exit a yard or building, not for parking or as a shortcut.
A tractor driver who obstructs traffic behind them must move to the right side of the road, using the hard shoulder if it is safe and necessary to let following traffic pass.
On a two-way road, the default rule for passing a structure, post, or closed area is to pass on the right side, unless a sign specifically indicates otherwise.
On a one-way road, since all traffic already moves in the same direction, passing an obstruction is permitted from either side by default, unless a sign specifically restricts it.
A category B driving license entitles its holder to drive any licensed invalid carriage with an all-up weight of up to 4,000 kg, as set out in the vehicle-class rules attached to that license.
A driver's license cannot be renewed without retesting once it has been expired for more than one full year, at which point the holder must pass the examinations required by the Licensing Authority.
In a properly functioning traffic light, the green light blinks three times as an advance warning before switching to yellow, giving drivers notice that the signal is about to change.
An ATV is legally permitted to travel on dirt roads and on roadways located within the boundaries of a Moshav or Kibbutz, reflecting its restricted off-road/rural use classification.

A vehicle non-use notice is issued directly to the driver by a policeman, a car assessor, or a driving examiner upon finding a malfunction or accident damage that makes the vehicle unfit for the road.
Carrying a passenger on an ATV is only permitted when the Licensing Authority has granted specific permission for it, as indicated on the vehicle's registration documents.
Wearing a helmet is mandatory for both the driver and every passenger while riding an ATV, given the vehicle's high rollover and ejection risk.
A utility vehicle, or mule, driver may carry a passenger only when the Licensing Authority has granted a permit allowing it, without which passenger transport is not allowed.
A utility vehicle is restricted by law to a maximum speed of 40 km/h on any type of road, consistent with its classification as a slow-moving vehicle.
Wearing safety belts in a utility vehicle is obligatory on every type of road, for both the driver and all passengers, without exception for off-road or short trips.
